title: Qualitative analysis of post-consumer and post-industrial waste via near-infrared, visual and induction identification with experimental sensor-based sorting setup
author: Friedrich, Koinig, et al.
materials: The next step is the setup of the system. In this case, three materials for creating the classification program are chosen: Polypropylene (PP), PET and thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU). Several pieces are taken and inserted into the experimental SBS setup to acquire an image and the corresponding NIR-spectra for each material. From the images of the pieces, several pixels are selected over which the respective NIR-spectrum is averaged. Fig. 6 shows the spectra of five selected pixels of a PP specimen. It can be seen that the spectra vary amongst those pixels although it is the same material. When selecting the areas of the particles, areas with reflections and edges should be avoided. The received spectrum is then assigned to the respective material. For the following comparison between the materials, the first derivative of the spectrum is used. The scattering of the spectra of the three materials is shown in Fig. 7, Fig. 8. As visible in the Fig.s, PET exhibits a relatively high scattering compared to the other two plastics. However, due to its characteristic peak in the area of 1650 nm, PET is usually easy to detect, especially in this case compared to PP and TPU.Fig. 6Scattering of the first derivative of the NIR-spectrum of PP amongst different Pixels (evaluation performed in MATLAB, authors depiction).Fig 6Fig. 7Scattering of the first derivative of the NIR-spectrum of PET (blue) (evaluation performed in MATLAB, authors depiction).Fig 7Fig. 8Scattering of the first derivative of the NIR-spectrum of yellow TPU (evaluation performed in MATLAB, authors depiction).Fig 8

steps.title: Prepare experimental SBS setup
steps.instruction: Assemble the two‑way sensor‑based sorting machine: place the vibrating conveyor (1) and the glass chute (2) as shown in Fig. 1, ensuring the grain‑size range of material to be processed is between 5 mm and 300 mm.

steps.title: Install illumination
steps.instruction: Mount the Helen Dr. Fischer 15026Z halogen lamp with reflector above the detection area, set its output to the maximum of 6.5 mW mm⁻² and adjust the dimming to obtain a flat NIR spectrum.

steps.title: Connect and verify sensors
steps.instruction: Connect the three sensors to the control cabinet: NIR EVK Helios G2‑320 (spectral range 930–1700 nm, scan rate 500 Hz full frame, resolution 9 nm, spectral sampling 3.1 nm, spatial resolution 312 px, pixel size 30 × 30 µm, C‑mount lens, slit 100 µm, GigE Vision & CamLink 2, RS‑485 trigger), VIS AViiVA® SC2 CL (resolution 1365 RGB pixels, pixel pitch 10 µm, line rate 14 kHz, output 12 bit, linearity <2 %, gain –2 dB to 22 dB, dynamic range 66 dB, PRNU ±4 %), and induction MESEP FS3 (sample rate 1 kHz, resolution 12–100 mm, baud 57 600–6 000 000, 4–124 channels). Verify Ethernet/R‑485 communication.

steps.title: Perform VIS white calibration
steps.instruction: Place the manufacturer‑provided white ceramic plate on the chute, capture an image with the VIS camera, and store it as the white reference for the colour model.

steps.title: Perform VIS black calibration
steps.instruction: Cover the VIS camera lens with a non‑permissive (black, carbon‑coloured) plate to block all light, capture an image and store it as the black reference.

steps.title: Perform NIR white calibration
steps.instruction: Place the same white ceramic plate on the chute, open EVK SQALAR, set the white calibration target to 2000 ALU (Arbitrary Light Units) and confirm.

steps.title: Perform NIR black calibration
steps.instruction: Block all incoming NIR light with a black polymer shield, start the black calibration in EVK SQALAR and set the lower threshold to 0 ALU.

steps.title: Define NIR background intensity
steps.instruction: In SQALAR, set the background intensity limit using the empty glass chute (2) as reference so that pixels below this limit are classified as background and ignored.

steps.title: Configure VIS HSV parameters
steps.instruction: Open the HSV configuration: set hue divisions to 48 units (0–360°), saturation scale to 200 units (0–100 %), and brightness scale to 250 units (0–100 %).

steps.title: Capture VIS images of reference plastics
steps.instruction: Insert separately a red LDPE, a white LDPE and a grey HDPE piece into the feed, let them pass the chute, and acquire a high‑resolution VIS image for each material.

steps.title: Create colour classes in Teachin ICC
steps.instruction: For each material image, load it into Teachin ICC, select a region of pixels that shows little reflection and is not at the edge, assign the corresponding hue, saturation and brightness values, and save the class. Repeat for all hue segments needed.

steps.title: Verify and optimise VIS coverage
steps.instruction: In Teachin ICC, view the coverage ratio of each colour class on the original image; if coverage is low (e.g., white or grey), add additional HSV ranges and weight the successful pixels twice for grey and white.

steps.title: Transfer VIS program to MMI
steps.instruction: Export the Teachin ICC colour model, import it into the machine‑machine interface (MMI), select the target material (white LDPE), and set the air‑nozzle pressure and the detection‑to‑ejection time delay Δt appropriate for the material’s fall speed.

steps.title: Run VIS sorting trial
steps.instruction: Feed the mixed plastic stream (Table 4) onto the vibrating conveyor, start the system, let the VIS sensor detect white LDPE pieces and trigger the corresponding air‑nozzle valve to eject them over the splitter; non‑target pieces fall into the reject box.

steps.title: Weigh VIS fractions
steps.instruction: Manually separate the ejected (target) and rejected (non‑target) fractions and record their masses to calculate throughput, purity, yield, recovery and incorrect discharges (see Tables 5‑6).

steps.title: Acquire NIR training spectra
steps.instruction: Place several pieces of polypropylene (PP), polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) on the chute, capture hyperspectral images with the EVK Helios NIR G2‑320, and select multiple pixels per piece avoiding edges and reflections.

steps.title: Process NIR spectra in MATLAB
steps.instruction: Export the HSI cube as a *.mat file, convert it to a grayscale intensity image, then for each selected pixel apply: first‑derivative, Gaussian smoothing with interval 10, and z‑score normalisation (mean 0, SD 1).

steps.title: Train NIR classification in SQALAR
steps.instruction: Load the processed spectra, assign each averaged spectrum to its material (PP, PET, TPU), select the wavelength range 930–1700 nm, and set the similarity threshold for class assignment.

steps.title: Verify NIR coverage and weighting
steps.instruction: Inspect the coverage ratios of the three materials; if necessary, adjust wavelength sections or increase weighting of well‑covered regions.

steps.title: Transfer NIR program to MMI
steps.instruction: Export the SQALAR classification, import it into the MMI, choose PP as the target material, and configure the same air‑nozzle pressure and Δt as used for VIS.

steps.title: Run NIR sorting trial
steps.instruction: Feed the mixed plastic stream (Table 4) onto the conveyor, start the system, let the NIR sensor detect PP pieces and trigger the air‑nozzle ejection; other plastics are rejected.

steps.title: Weigh NIR fractions
steps.instruction: Manually separate and weigh target and non‑target fractions; record the data for throughput, purity, yield, recovery and incorrect discharges (Tables 7‑8).

steps.title: Set induction sensor parameters
steps.instruction: On the MMI, program the induction sensor (MESEP FS3) with: delay time 65 ms, minimum blow‑out time 15 ms, minimum object size 3 mm, scaling 100 %, edge valves ON, sensitivity 35 (range 5–750).

steps.title: Run induction sorting trial
steps.instruction: Feed the refuse‑derived fuel (RDF) stream onto the conveyor, start the system, let the induction sensor detect metallic objects and activate the compressed‑air nozzle bar to eject them over the splitter; non‑metallic material falls to the reject bin.

steps.title: Weigh induction fractions
steps.instruction: Manually separate target metal and reject fractions, weigh each, and log throughput, purity, yield, recovery and incorrect discharges (Tables 9‑10).

steps.title: Configure sensor‑fusion model
steps.instruction: Combine the VIS colour model for white glass, the NIR models for plastics, and set the induction sensor to a negative (no‑metal) condition; import all three models into the MMI.

steps.title: Run sensor‑fusion sorting trial
steps.instruction: Feed the mixed input (Table 11) onto the conveyor, start the system, and allow the combined sensors to eject only white glass pieces while rejecting all plastics, coloured glass, metals and other materials.

steps.title: Weigh sensor‑fusion fractions
steps.instruction: Separate and weigh the ejected white‑glass fraction and the reject fraction; record performance metrics (throughput, purity, yield, recovery, incorrect discharges) as shown in Tables 12‑13.

steps.title: Record performance metrics for all trials
steps.instruction: For each of the VIS (10 trials), NIR (10 trials), induction (10 trials) and sensor‑fusion (10 trials) experiments, enter the following data into a spreadsheet: time of experiment (s), input mass (kg), mass of eject (kg), mass of reject (kg), target material in eject (kg), target material in reject (kg), non‑target material in eject (kg), non‑target material in reject (kg), throughput‑rate (kg h⁻¹ m⁻¹), purity (%), yield (%), recovery (%), incorrect discharges (%). Use the exact numbers from Tables 5‑6, 7‑8, 9‑10 and 12‑13.

description: Sensor-based sorting is used in waste management for sorting and analysing waste streams and bulk materials. It is a non-contact, non-destructive process that offers a great deal of flexibility to cope with a wide variety of tasks. The Chair for Waste Processing Technology and Waste Management (AVAW) has an experimental sensor-based sorting setup for university and industrial research projects designed as a two-way machine. A grain size range from 5 to 300 mm can be processed. The feed takes place via a vibrating conveyor (1) followed by a glass chute (2) (see Fig. 1). The experimental sensor-based sorting (SBS) setup contains three sensors (referred to Fig. 1) that can be used for different waste streams:-Near-infrared sensor (NIR) (5): waste glass, paper and cardboard, plastics, electronic scrap as well as construction and demolition waste.-High-resolution colour line scan camera with the measurement principle of visual spectroscopy (VIS) (5): plastics, wood, paper and cardboard, waste glass as well as construction and demolition waste.-Electromagnetic induction sensor (3): electric conductors, e.g. metallic waste.Fig. 1Functional schematic of the experimental sensor-based sorting setup at AVAW [3].Fig 1 It is also possible to combine several sensors to solve complex tasks with so-called sensor fusion. Currently, norms are existing how to interpret NIR spectra with standard test methods like ASTM D 1925 Determination Yellowness Index or ASTM D 1003 Haze and Luminous Transmittance of Transparent Plastics, but none how to record all the data (VIS, NIR, induction, senor fusion) for such a setup, which is the focused method in this research paper [1,2]. In order to reproduce all applicable methods with the experimental SBS setup, the specifications of the sensors are listed.
